title: Ninth Circuit vacates Amazon's injunction against Perplexity's Comet, rules users access sites — not AI agents
subtitle: The August 4 panel opinion by Judge Milan D. Smith Jr. applies the rule of lenity to the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, holding Amazon is unlikely to prove Perplexity itself accessed Amazon.com when Comet acts on user instructions — the first published circuit ruling on AI-agent liability under the CFAA.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on August 4 vacated the preliminary injunction Amazon had won against Perplexity's Comet shopping agent. The panel, in an opinion authored by Circuit Judge Milan D. Smith Jr., held that Amazon is unlikely to succeed on the merits of its Computer Fraud and Abuse Act claim because Comet is a tool operated by users, not by Perplexity itself. The court applied the rule of lenity — the principle that ambiguity in a criminal statute is construed against liability — and explicitly acknowledged there is "little to no existing caselaw directly dealing with how to ascribe responsibility for AI agents" under the CFAA. Amazon had sued Perplexity in November 2025, arguing that automated agents accessing Amazon.com and private account information must transparently identify themselves as bots. The Electronic Frontier Foundation had filed an amicus brief supporting Perplexity and the ruling largely tracks its arguments.

The legal mechanism matters because the CFAA is the primary federal statute used to constrain automated web access, and its "exceeds authorized access" clause is the tool of choice for site operators trying to block scrapers, crawlers, and — now — AI agents. By holding that the user, not the tool-maker, is the party who accesses the third-party site, the Ninth Circuit has drawn a line that is directly analogous to how the courts have long treated web browsers. The opinion effectively says: if Firefox is not liable when you use it to visit a site you were not supposed to, Comet is not liable when you use it to shop on a site whose terms disfavor agents. Whether the user themselves has authorized access is a separate question the ruling leaves open for future litigation.

The broader significance is that this is the first published circuit-level opinion to squarely address AI-agent liability under the CFAA — the statute agentic-AI startups have been most worried about. Anthropic's Computer Use, OpenAI's Operator, Perplexity's Comet, and every browser-driving agent behind them have been operating in a grey zone where a hostile injunction could shut down a product overnight. The Ninth Circuit's ruling narrows that risk considerably within its jurisdiction, which covers California, Washington, and most of the West Coast — the geography where these products are built. It does not resolve the parallel questions under state trespass-to-chattels doctrine or under the sites' contractual terms of service, both of which Amazon can still pursue. But on the federal criminal-statute question, the direction of travel is now visible: the user is the accessor, the agent is the tool.

For learners: the interesting sentence in the opinion is the acknowledgment that there is almost no caselaw on ascribing responsibility for AI agents. That is not a limitation, it is an invitation. The doctrines that will govern autonomous software — CFAA, agency law, product liability, professional responsibility for agents acting on behalf of a client — are being drafted in real time, one panel opinion at a time. If you are early in a legal, policy, or engineering career and you want to work on questions that will shape the next twenty years of the industry, this is the frontier. Read the opinion itself; the primary source is more accessible than most, and the reasoning generalizes well beyond shopping agents.
